newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil coffee traders ask: How far can market go?
newsitem.headline: Brazil coffee traders ask: How far can market go?

text.p: The recent meteoric rise in world coffee prices has left traders in Brazil and elsewhere in the coffee community wondering how much more the market can absorb.

Colombia's Finance Minister has already voiced his concern this week about "excessive" coffee prices and the threat they pose to long-term consumption patterns and this view is shared by Brazil's coffee roasters.

"Over $2 a lb is starting to get to dangerous levels. It is too high and will start to be reflected in world consumption," said Americo Sato, vice-president of the Brazilian Coffee Industry Association.
For the time being, there is little sign of a slackening in demand for Brazilian coffee.

Brazil had been expected to struggle to meet a six million bag export quota set by the Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) in January to June but the current rate of exports suggests that this will be easily achieved and possibly even exceeded.
February shipments are now expected to be in excess of one million 60-kg bags and could even exceed January's 1.25 million bags despite the shorter working month and the Carnival holidays.
As of February 4, February bills of lading totalled 1.05 million bags while 1.32 million bags had been registered for shipment, according to a report by Santos export firm Icatu/Sumatra.
"We expect March at 1.45 million bags of green coffee. Brazil will continue actively selling as far as availability permits," the report said.
The big question now is what is that availability, with traders increasingly moving towards crop estimates for the 1996/97 harvest of 27 million to 28 million bags and some even beyond.

Exports are not being carried out at the expense of internal demand as roasters are still able to get hold of coffee in the domestic market, albeit at high prices, the Sao Paulo Coffee Industry Union said earlier this week.
A near sell-out in the March 5 government stock auction should lead to a larger sale in April but even so, the total is not likely to exceed 300,000 bags, Sato said.
If Brazil continues to supply the world market with perhaps larger quantities of 1996/97 coffee than originally anticipated, would this be enough to start bringing prices down again?
The answer may be yes if a larger-than-expected crop in 1996/97 means a larger-than-expected harvest in 1997/98.
"If we are looking at 28 million bags plus, then 25 million to 26 million bags in 1997/98 is not inconceivable," one analyst said.
But Brazil watchers have all too often seen logic and reason go out the window as the frost season approaches and prices heat up as temperatures drop.
"We have all been expecting liquidation/profit-taking at some point. $2 a lb was a target, it was surpassed and now what have we?," said the Icatu/Sumatra report.

"Most probably wherever the retracement happens, New York will be brought back up again during the nervous Brazilian winter. The importance of the trend today is based on fundamentals and pure psychological forces," it added.
